subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, BOUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that the governor in council may do such things as to him appear to be necessary for carrying into effect the treaties of peace between Canada and Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland, respectively; and for that purpose the governor in council may make appointments, establish offices and make orders or regulations; and to provide further that any expense incurred in carrying out the treaties shall be defrayed out of moneys voted by parliament.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Mr. Chairman, this resolution is for leave to introduce a bill consequent upon the action taken in the house

Treaties oj Peace
during the last session with respect to the treaties between Canada and Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland. Hon. members will recall that these treaties were approved by resolutions of both houses of parliament. Subsequent to the approval, ratifications by His Majesty on the advice of the Canadian government were deposited in the manner required by the treaties to bring them into operation. It is now felt desirable to have legislation passed which will enable , the governor in council to take from time to time whatever action may be required to give effect to the provisions of the treaties.
The bill to be introduced following upon this resolution will be in substance similar to the bills that were passed after the last war, one of them being chapter 30 of the statutes of 1919, another chapter 4 of the statutes of 1920, and the third chapter 49 of the statutes of 1922. It is also in substance similar to the bill which was passed almost a year ago, I think, by the parliament of the United Kingdom. I understand a similar bill is now before the parliament of the commonwealth of New Zealand.
The terms of the bill are in substance exactly the same as those of the bills which were thus adopted to empower the governor in council to do whatever might be required to carry out the provisions of the treaty. Hon. members will recall that the British system is not the same as the United States system, where a treaty automatically, upon approval, becomes the law of the land.
Last year parliament' was asked to approve these treaties. That makes them binding obligations between this country and the other party to the treaty, but it does not constitute legislation effective upon Canadian citizens; and this procedure is the one that it is usual to adopt in connection with the implementation of treaties, after they have become binding between this country and the other party thereto.

subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, BOUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND
speechtext:
Will the minister say if the implementation of the treaty raises the vexed question of jurisdiction between the dominion and the provinces?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That question might arise if the governor in council did adopt orders in council to implement the treaties which in their effect trenched upon property and civil rights in the provinces. But, of course, no action taken here, or no action taken by the government, could be effective if it was not within the constitutional powers of the authority taking the action. For instance, there is a provision in these treaties that the period of the war is not to operate
for the purpose of the application of the statute of limitations. That may very well be something that is within provincial jurisdiction, and the question might arise whether any order in council passed by federal authority under the statute that it is proposed to ask parliament to adopt was valid or not. In our own jurisdiction, Quebec, I think that the interruption of prescription would be automatic, because of the impossibility of a creditor, affected by the state of war, pursuing his recourse. Our code provides that whenever the creditor is prevented from exercising his right, the period of limitation against him does not run. That is the general principle which is embodied in the treaties here. There were similar provisions in the treaties made after the first world war. There was an order in council which purported to make them effective, and I do not think any litigation arose over them.

subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, BOUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND
speechtext:
The minister will recall that a number of statutes which were enacted by the government led by Mr. Bennett, as he then was, were attacked because their jurisdiction rested upon that clause in the British North America Act which purported to empower this parliament to enact legislation giving effect to treaties. We know what answer the courts gave in those cases. I want to know whether the present government would be relying upon an emergency, for instance, to enact legislation which it could not enact under the section of the British North America Act as interpreted by the courts when, they disallowed the Bennett legislation.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Oh, no. There is no assertion of a constitutional principle here. This is merely empowering legislation to authorize the governor in council to do what parliament might do by specific legislation in each instance.
As a matter of fact I inquired if there had been very much that had to be done after the first world war to implement the treaties. I found that in fact there was very little, but there was something done, and there will have to be something done at this time, to deal with property which during the war was vested in the hands of the custodian of enemy property. There are matters of that kind which do arise and with which it is necessary to deal. But there is a special provision here, because I wanted to anticipate any objection that might arise in that connection, that any order in council will have to be tabled in parliament within a fortnight if parliament is in session, and if not, within the first fifteen days of the next ensuing session.
Treaties of Peace

subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, BOUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND
speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the minister to the fact that Canada has been at peace with these countries since the close of the German war. In the first place since the end of the war these countries, or three of them, have become Soviet satellite countries. I refer to Roumania, Hungary and Finland. What is the policy of the government with regard to some of these changes that will have to be made in the treaty as a result of Soviet action?
In the second place, I was opposed to the doctrine that Canada could sign these treaties separately from the mother country. Canada secured that right back in the early twenties. At that time we got the power to sign treaties as Canada, separately from Britain. We have been at peace with these countries for years, but they have now become Soviet satellite countries. Finland is a Soviet satellite. Russia has secured a port at Petsamo in Finland. What they want it for I do not know. Roumania has become a Soviet satellite nation, and so has Hungary.
I am opposed to the policy of our dealing with a matter such as this at this time. At Lake Success, where these matters are supposed to be discussed, a stand should have been taken regarding these nations. All the scare and all the clamour raised by Russia at Lake Success was for home consumption in Russia, where, if they had been left alone by the UNO, the people had enough trouble of their own to occupy their attention.
The government should give us further information in this matter if we are to establish offices in these different places, though I do not see why they want to do so. Who wants to go to any Russian satellite country such as Roumania or Hungary at a time like this? These countries are Soviet police states; that is all they are. They are absolutely under the control of this dictator country.
Clemenceau said that Britain was the most difficult country in the world to make treaties with because it always speaks with so many voices. We have no navy, army, or air force; we have no means by which to protect our interests with these people at the present time. As I said last night, if Lake Success were to be closed for a year or even six months we might begin to talk about redeeming some of these countries, which are simply police states under Russia. If we were going to sign treaties with these nations why have we waited for two or three years to execute them? As far as Canada is concerned, this is a separate nation under the act that was passed away back in 1921 or 1922. I do not know why

we have waited for three or four years to sign treaties which were ready two or three years ago. Why bring it up now? As for establishing offices in these countries, you are simply going to get into trouble. I was glad to see my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) go over to Moscow as a delegate from the dominion, but at the time, on one occasion when he was speaking to a former minister of health, I suggested that the government had better send over a bodyguard with him because I was afraid they might kidnap him while he was in Moscow.

subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, BOUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND
speechtext:
I remember that in August 1940 there was quite a fight for the prorogation of parliament, but instead of that, parliament was adjourned so that the members could be called together at any time to decide important matters during the war. There was a special session in November of that year and it was adjourned, and during the adjournment Canada declared war on five countries. I have never understood why a declaration of war on any country was not a grave enough matter to call the members of parliament together at any time of the year, but during that brief period of time, shortly after the adjournment, Canada declared war on five countries. And still we call ourselves a peace-loving nation.
Not only that, but what business did we have to declare war on Roumania, Hungary and Finland? We did not send a man to fight them. We did not send a plane. We were at war with these nations because the United Kingdom had declared war. This is something I have not understood on the part of a peace-loving nation. The declaration of war on Italy had a certain sense, and our boys went there to fight on the soil of Italy.
One day I telephoned the Department of External Affairs and asked one of the higher-ups to tell me with what countries we were at war. He replied, "Wait a minute; I am not sure about that. You had better ask somebody else". I had to telephone two or three of the higher-ups to find out with what countries I as a Canadian citizen was at war. I did not know with whom I was at war and I could not be told by the experts.
If the name of Bulgaria does not appear here, with Italy, Hungary and Finland, it is because Bulgaria was forgotten by the experts in the Department of External Affairs when Canada ceased for a moment to be a peace-loving nation. But we continue to consider these men as experts. I have the highest regard for my chief, the Prime Minister; I have the highest regard for the present Secre-

Treaties of Peace
tary of State for External Affairs, but I ask them to get rid of the nonentities in the Department of External Affairs, who take themselves so seriously.
Imagine! The more countries we are at war with the greater country is Canada. I afterwards asked how many men we had sent there and what we had done to fight them. Nothing at all. But we were at war. This is idle talk, and I wonder what the influence of Canada is in the drafting of these treaties. Did Canada dot an "i" or cross a "t" in the manufacture of those treaties? Canada had nothing to do. We have the role of suiveux, blind followers, in all these treaties. If Canada had had something to do with the discussion of these treaties, with the ratification of them, we could consider the thing seriously; but I remember reading not long ago that my right hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs had complained about the fact that Canada was not consulted at all concerning the manufacture of treaties-the fabrication of treaties. It was left to the big powers. That is why I find the set-up of the united nations is all wrong. It is because the basis of the united nations is not the basis of right, it is not the basis of justice. It is the basis of might, the same that prevailed in Germany at the time of the kaiser. Might is right. These big ones do everything.
Have we heard that any country besides the big ones had anything to do with it? Moreover, an important senator was silly enough to say that the Prime Minister would lead the small nations at San Francisco. This made me so indignant, to think that Canada was a small nation. That such a thing was said by a cabinet minister who has a seat in the senate was an insult to all of us, because Canada is not a small country. Canada is a great country. If Canada is merely a small country it was not led by the Prime Minister at San Francisco, although I suggested in the spring of 1945 that the Prime Minister should be made president of the conference at San Francisco. At the time he was not interested in having that presidency, but it would have been worthy of him, a man of his experience, who has occupied the post of Prime Minister longer than any man within the British empire has held such an office.
Therefore, sir, I find all the discussion concerning international affairs childish. It is not serious. This was-with Hungary, with Rou-mania, with Finland-a theoretical war, a war on paper. How is it that a peace-loving nation decides to declare war and do nothing afterwards? It is shadow-boxing in order to give the illusion that we are prizefighters. That is all it is. Roumania owes Canada $20,000,000 plus compound interest over the period since
the first war. I wonder if Russia is ready to endorse Roumania's note to Canada for that amount? Twenty million dollars is a large sum of money. It represents the amount of money that Canada has voted for the children of Europe. Why do we not get something from Roumania? If Roumanian people have property here, why do we not confiscate it in payment of the amount which has been due to us for such a long time? There was gold here which was deposited in Canada by debtor countries. Why do we not hold what we can get to compensate us for the sacrifices we have made and the loans that we have made to all the nations of the wrnrld?
I shall not say any more about the matter, as I do not want to carry the discussion too far. But if all these things are to be adopted, they should be adopted as a matter of course or as a matter of routine, because we had nothing to do with the making of the treaties and nothing to do with the actual war with those countries. It is a great mistake to follow blindly the external policy of the United Kingdom. Why? Because the independent nations will consider Canada as a satellite of England just as the Ukraine, Roumania, Hungary and Finland-although Finland not so much-are supposed to be satellites of Russia. If we act with regard to Great Britain in the same way as the satellite countries act with regard to Russia, we shall be considered by the rest of the world as a satellite of England and we shall deserve their contempt. It would be much better for Great Britain if there were more vigour and independence in the external policy of the dominions of the British commonwealth. Australia set a great example during the post-war period. Australia was respected by the whole world, even by those who did not agree with her policy.
I believe that each one of us should have pride in his country, that he should be a Canadian first and should be ashamed to follow blindly the long and winding policy made by the long-beards of the foreign office. They have been instrumental in the disruption that is taking place now throughout the world. Their policies were responsible for the massacre of Turkey a- long time ago, of India, of Palestine, and for the division and disruption of the British empire.
We are a young nation. Let us show that we can lead the world in the path of honesty and order. We shall never do so if we follow blindly the policies, full of intrigue, of other countries.

With respect to the German treaty, the government of Canada has taken the position that in the preparation of the final treaty it should have a part commensurate with the part we took in the war. That is still the attitude that is being maintained. At the present time, however, negotiations are going on between the powers occupying the western zone-the United States, the United Kingdom and France-for not a permanent but rather a semi-permanent solution for the western zone, pending the time when a general treaty, or the possibility of making a general treaty, can be envisaged. In the preparation of these semi-permanent solutions, these powers have seen fit to accept the intervention of the Benelux countries, which border upon western Germany. We have been kept informed of what has been going on, and we have not insisted on being present at that stage because if we did it would be a reason for bringing in a great many other countries, which might hamper or retard the progress being made in trying to bring some semblance of order and reorganization into this zone-a very important zone not only to the Germans who inhabit it, but to the whole of western Europe. Its restoration, not to the extent of becoming again a menace to its neighbours but to the extent of taking its part in the integrated economies of western Europe, is important to the whole of western Europe; and because it is important to the whole of western Europe it is of direct interest to us.
For that reason we have not wished to appear to be attempting to put forward technical claims which might require the occupying powers, in order to give offence to no one, to invite all those who had declared war against Germany; this in our opinion would have had a delaying effect on the measures the occupying powers are trying to take to bring about some semi-permanent solution of the problem. But we are still insisting that when it comes

to the making of the final peace with Germany the powers who took a substantial part in the winning of the war shall be given a role proportionate to their importance in the conflict.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the questions which have been directed to the ministry with regard to these treaties relate to what grew out of the meeting of the council of foreign ministers at Potsdam in 1945 and the conference held in Paris in 1946. At that conference, as hon. members know, the Canadian delegation was headed by the Prime Minister until his departure for Canada, when it became my honour and privilege to succeed him.
This matter has been before the house on several occasions already. In an appendix to Votes and Proceedings for February 10, 1947, will be found a report from myself to the Secretary of State for External Affairs on
the work done at the conference. On March 3, 1947, as reported at page 952 of Hansard, I made some remarks in the 'house on the work of the conference and what was done by the Canadian delegation there. If my recollection serves me aright, though I would have to check this again, there was some further discussion on June 30, 1947.
With regard first to the nature of the conference, in those statements there will be found a thorough-going criticism of the adequacy of the conference and of that kind of treatymaking. What is more, that criticism was voiced not in Canada alone but also at the conference itself, by the Prime Minister while he was there and by myself. The views that were then advanced received support not only from representatives of the middle and smaller powers there, but also from some of the greater powers.
I am sure it is not the wish of hon. members that I should delay these proceedings except to refresh their memories by these references. But when we come to consider Canada's interests with regard to these treaties I think once more we must recall the fact that the first Canadian corps constituted the third largest force which fought the whole long way from Sicily almost to the banks of the Po in Italy, and that the graves of more than five thousand Canadians who gave their lives in that fight remain in Italian soil. If anyone should question our interest in this, apart from the fact that Canada made a major contribution to victory on the Mediterranean front, then I would reply that this interest was not questioned at Paris. It was interesting to note how day after day we would be carrying on our deliberations at the Luxembourg, and in between those deliberations the nations interested in the outcome of these treaties would be sending in their recommendations and sending around their delegations in order that they might have our understanding, our sympathy and if possible our support for the points of view they were putting forward.
With regard to our interest in declaring war on Roumania, which was the question raised by the hon. member for Temiscouata-and a very natural and proper question-at the moment I do not know how many members of the Royal Canadian Air Force flew over Roumania or Hungary or some of these other countries during the war. There were quite enough of them, however, to make it important for them and for us to see that in case of a forced landing in those countries they should have the rights accorded to belligerents. Without these declarations of war our men
Treaties of Peace

flying those planes, on missions which undoubtedly were of the utmost importance in the allied cause, when forced to land might have been treated quite differently from the treatment they received as belligerents. When you get men of this type undertaking missions of that kind, men with the kind of courage required to fly off into night and space, even beyond the range of the normal flight of their planes, it is up to us to give them protection. They were belligerents fighting for us, declared to be such and recognized as such. I am sure that the hon. member for Temis-couata will recognize that from the national and patriotic and humanitarian point of view that is a sufficient answer. It is certainly the answer which, as Minister of National Defence, I would wish to give.
With regard to our exploits in these fields I would draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that there has been delivered to them a book entitled, "The Canadian Army, Official War Summary". This was issued just today, almost three years from the termination of hostilities in Europe. I think hon. members will find in this book a true and fine objective account of the exploits of our soldiers in the fields of action to which these treaties relate. The navy and air force stories will come later.
All three branches did their part in bringing about a cessation of hostilities so that we might have formal peace with these countries, in the hope that from that peace we might build a foundation for a better future, not only for the countries themselves but for our own country. Our interest demands that there should be peace in these countries as well as here, and that just as soon as possible trade should be established on a sound basis with those countries as well as with all other countries.
In the prosecution of that end, your delegation, first under the Prime Minister and then under my direction, worked steadfastly at Paris. I believe we made a contribution similar to that made by the seventeen powers who were not great powers. I believe we earned the respect of the countries with whom we were working. I believe that if you compare the draft treaties and the discussion with the final treaties as signed you will see that there was some improvement. There was not nearly as much improvement as we would have liked, nor was it the kind of conference which we would have liked or which we hope will be set up with respect to the treaties of peace with Germany and Japan. But in consequence of the discussions at Paris the treaties were better than they would have been had the representatives of the seventeen smaller powers not been there.

Had we not been represented and taken as effective a part as we could in the discussions at Paris the people of Canada would have been the first to say that we were remiss in our duty. We did the utmost we could within the terms of reference, working in close co-operation with the other countries that were there. We achieved something, but not nearly as much as we would have liked. Our hope is that the views expressed by Canada at Paris, and since, will have some influence in persuading the three or four great powers that we should have a more effective voice in future treaty making, and that the part we played in the war must be fully and adequately represented in the part we can play in building the foundations of peace.

There may be confusion between two kinds of suggestions. When I said that I had made suggestions, I was replying to some criticism offered, I believe, by the hon. members for Rosetown-Biggar and Peel and other hon. members of the procedure when the matter came before the house last year. At that time we made some suggestions as to the kind of procedure that should be followed in making treaties of this type.
Treaties oj Peace

With regard to suggestions on the five draft treaties that were before the conference, the draft treaties were under discussion for some three months. They had been prepared by the council of foreign ministers, representing the United Kingdom, the United States, the Soviet Union, and France. Those drafts were put before the conference, to which were summoned seventeen other powers, including Canada. The countries there represented had an opportunity of putting forward their views.
The conference was divided into some nine commissions, and views were put forward with respect to many of the provisions of all of the treaties. The discussions went on in the commissions, and I think it would be a fair estimate to say that altogether there were something over one thousand votes taken on the recommendations that might be made by the conference with regard to the text of the treaties. Those votes were cast by the Canadian delegation, as by the other countries represented, according to their instructions and in the light of the best information they had.
The countries there assembled included the United States of America, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, Ethiopia, France, Great Britain, Greece, India, Norway, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Poland, Czechoslovakia, the Ukraine, Union of South Africa, the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia.
It would be easy, if it were desirable, to go back over the records, which- are very full, to indicate how the Canadian delegation voted on each one of the issues put forward in each of these nine commissions each day of the conference. The member for Temiscouata did not ask me to do that in his first speech, and hon. members will agree that I answered the questions he put in his first speech just as adequately as they could be answered. But if for any reason he is interested in learning how the Canadian delegation voted on each one of the points put forward with regard to each separate section of each of the five treaties, the records will show that; and if he so desires we shall be prepared to defend each one of those votes as we go along, just as we did in consultation with the other nations represented at Paris. We played the same part that any nation would, faced with that situation at Paris. We heard the discussions, we received our instructions, we considered the situation, and we voted on each point as it came up.
In the final session, in the last three days I believe, hon. members might be surprised to learn that there were something like 250 or 300 votes on different points that had been raised in the different commissions.
We have a record of this as well. If anyone likes to see it he can do so, but he will

not be able to do very much about the terms of these treaties. We have passed the resolution through the house. The treaties have been signed, and now we are face to face with one thing only, namely, whether or not a bill will be passed, after its introduction, to carry into effect those treaties in so far as they are necessary to be carried into effect in Canada.
The hon. member for Temiscouata might have made these points in March or June of last year. If he has any desire for information I have the records to give to him, but I do not see that I need detain the committee with that exercise at this time.

speechtext:
This resolution has to do with Canada's part in administering certain treaties of peace with Roumania, Hungary, Finland and Italy. There are three sections to the resolution. I should like to ask the minister one question with respect to each of them. These questions have to do more with procedure and administration than with the terms of the treaties themselves.
The first section of the resolution reads as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that the governor in council may do such things as to him may appear to be necessary . . .
My first question is a very simple one. Why is it necessary that there be a resolution at this time? Why not the bill itself? I can understand that under our procedure a money bill has to be preceded by a resolution. I am asking only for information. No doubt the minister can give it without much difficulty.
My second question has to do with the suggestion in the latter part of the first third of the resolution, and with respect to the second part of the resolution which reads as follows:
... do such things as to him appear to be necessary for carrying into effect the treaties of peace between Canada and Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland, respectively; and for that purpose the governor in council may make appointments, establish offices and make orders or regulations.
My question is, what is the nature of the work to be done? Perhaps the minister can briefly give the committee in simple language some idea of the work that is contemplated under the bill which will be introduced.
The third part of the resolution has to do with the matter of expenditures and reads as follows:
And to provide further that any expense incurred in carrying out the treaties shall be defrayed out of moneys voted by parliament.

Treaties of Peace
Will the minister indicate whether these expenditures are likely to be large or small sums, whether they are to deal only with the personnel of the department for carrying out certain instructions, or are any large sums likely to be involved?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: May I deal with the questions in the reverse order from that in which they were put? The first has to do with what is contemplated as expenditures. I would imagine that there would be very little, possibly none at all, but the law officers of the house are very careful that there should be a resolution wherever there is any chance that the legislation to be brought down may involve the expenditure of money, because of the requirements of the British North America Act that such legislation be preceded by a resolution. They take no chances because, they say, if it did happen that money was involved, the legislation would be invalid if it had not been preceded by a resolution. There is apt to be very little, if any, and that is why the bill is drawn in the way that if there is any it will have to be by appropriation of parliament.
We do not intend this to be a bill authorizing the expenditure of money. There may be some of the time of employees taken in dealing with various aspects of the liquidation of enemy property, and things of that kind; but if anything required money that was not in the ordinary administrative vote of the department there would have to be a special appropriation by parliament, and it would have to be by a special item in the estimate.

subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, BOUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND
speechtext:
The minister does not contemplate anything more than a minor increase in expenditure?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: A very minor increase in expenditure. The nature of the things that may have to be done cannot be determined in an all-inclusive way. The treaties in question provide that enemy property now vested in the custodian may be confiscated and the proceeds retained by us and applied to settle any debt owing to a Canadian for some damage suffered by him as a consequence of the war. There are certain assets which are in the control of the custodian. It will probably be necessary, as it was after the other war, to have someone designated to advertise for claims, to receive the claims, to determine how they will be dealt with for the purpose of ascertaining their validity or not, and then to determine whether there is enough to satisfy them all, or whether there will be only a pro rata payment to each, if the amounts claimed are larger than the amounts available for distribution, and things of that kind.
Then there are provisions in the treaty relating to patents that may have been in existence, valid in this country, in favour of persons who became enemy aliens. Some of those have been taken as enemy property and disposed of. There are matters of that kind. These provisions are reciprocal. There may be Canadians who have rights in enemy countries. Those rights are restored by the treaty, but on a reciprocal basis. Therefore, in order to get for Canadian citizens, for instance, the benefit of a patent a Canadian citizen may have operative in Italy, we have to do something reciprocal for an Italian who may have had a patent operative in Canada. It is matters of that kind which do not affect the relations of governments with each other as such, but which affect the interests of the subjects of the countries which were at war and which are now at peace as a consequence of the treaties and the ratification thereof last September after the house had authorized the ratification.

If we did make a mistake and legislation was passed which should have had a resolution it would be invalid because of the terms of the British North America Act. They say, we would rather have you pass a resolution which may not be necessary than take any risk of passing a bill without one and have it decided afterwards that it required a resolution.

speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1944, and in particular to authorize approved lending institutions to purchase from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages held by the said corporation and to make loans to owners of rental housing projects not exceeding in amount 85 per cent of the estimated cost thereof; to authorize Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to guarantee an annual return of an amount to be determined by the corporation of rentals from rental housing projects for a period not exceeding thirty years, to make loans to owners of rental housing projects if such loans are not being made available by approved lending institutions; to authorize the governor in council to transfer lands vested in His Majesty to the corporation; and to make provision for the winding-up and dissolution of Wartime Housing Limited and to vest in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation power to provide rental housing out of moneys which may be appropriated by parliament for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OP APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes.

National Housing Act
Before dealing with the legislation proposed in this resolution I would like to comment briefly upon the general housing situation.
Continuing high levels of employment and income, and the high marriage rate, are currently, as in the last few years, placing great pressures on the housing supply. There is still congestion in many parts of the country, and in spite of a large number of new units in 1947 there is much doubling up and over-crowding.
However, in 1947 considerable progress was made. Hon. members will recall that I expressed the hope that the completion of
80.000	units would take place in 1947. Figures recently released by the dominion bureau of statistics indicate completions of 77,000 units. There were about 79,000 starts during the calendar year. The carry-over, or incomplete construction, of 42,000 units was slightly increased over the 40,000 at the end of last year. For the first time since war began, new housing units exceeded net family formation. The margin was about 13,000 units.
Although the objective or target of 80,000 units was substantially accomplished, it by no means solved the over-crowded housing situation. Furthermore, during the last year the cost of construction has risen sharply. Our costs of rental units are about 15 per cent higher than a year ago. In spite of the resulting higher sale prices, the effective demand for home ownership continues. The number of completed but unsold houses is relatively small. For instance, in the city of Vancouver, where proportionately there is more new housing than in any other place in the dominion, completed but unsold houses amount to less than one week's supply of new houses. The same situation pertains generally throughout the country.
I would point out, however, that the greatest demand and need is for rental housing. Many people buying houses are only doing so because they cannot secure rented accommodation. Although the 77.000 completions were large in number, only 22,000 of these units were for rental. The balance were built by or for home owners. Of the 22,000 rental units, some 13,000 were built under government sponsorship. This includes wartime housing units, units constructed by housing enterprises, and our emergency shelter activities. For reasons which I will discuss later there was relatively little activity by the entrepreneur in the rental field. I will be suggesting steps which may be taken to help remedy this deficiency.
Housing completions in 1947 were the largest on record in any one year. This was achieved at a time when capital investment 5849-231
of other forms was at unprecedented levels. By various means the dominion government provided assistance for about one-third of the 1947 housing program. The large number of completions was only possible because the government took very positive steps to facilitate the flow of materials. These steps were of great assistance to private enterprise which saw to the major portion of the 1947 program. Some of these steps included the encouragement of additional production of our shortest items such as soil pipe and plumbing fixtures. As a result of arrangements with the steel companies, the supply of nails was maintained at a very high level. Our policy in respect to timber exports resulted in a sufficient supply of lumber to meet the largest capital investment program we have ever experienced.
As evidence of the beneficial effects of these steps, the average time of construction for a residential unit was substantially reduced. One sample indicates the average time of construction reduced from eleven months in 1946 to eight months in 1947. This reduced time represents a saving in construction cost. This reduction in time of construction has offset, in part, increases in price of building materials and wage costs of about 18 per cent in 1947. I am glad to report that the efforts of my department to secure a greater and more regular flow of building materials have had beneficial effects.
I would now like to deal with the highlights of some of the direct operations by government in the housing field. In 1946 we took vigorous steps to provide emergency shelter units in those communities where there was heavy congestion. These steps were continued in 1947, during which time some 3,800 units were brought into occupancy. In all, through the assistance rendered under the emergency shelter regulations, some 10,000 units have been provided to relieve the most overcrowded conditions. In this work we have had a very full measure of co-operation from municipalities. The present situation is that we have used up practically all surplus buildings suitable for the purpose. But there are indications that the greatest need for emergency shelter is past.
In our rental housing program in 1947, 5,421 units were completed, and we had a carryover of 5,354 units, most of which will be completed during the first half of 1948.
On October 10, 1947, I announced the terms of the 1948 rental program. The arrangement is more favourable to the municipalities than previous operations by Wartime Housing Limited. The type of unit conforms more
National Housing Act

closely to current residential development. Arrangements are made with the municipality so that these houses may be sold. Agreements have now been signed for 3,575 units, and negotiations are under way for 5,179 units. By regions the number of units under signed agreements or negotiations, as at April 23, are:
Maritimes, 1,319; Quebec, 415; Ontario, 3,375; Prairies, 2,530; British Columbia, 1,115.
Because we do not wish to enter into winter construction involving extra costs, we will be following the custom of the last two years in accepting applications from municipalities up to June 1, 194S. Whether the dominion will continue in the direct rental field in 1949 is a matter for further consideration. But we will not enter into construction in 1948 unless municipalities make arrangements for rental housing before June 1, 1948.
At the time I announced the 1948 rental program, I expressed the hope that we might complete arrangements for 12,000 units. From the figures which I have already given you, you will notice that a small proportion of the units are in the province of Quebec. Little success has attended our efforts to arrange agreements with municipalities in that province.
Under legislation brought down by the Ontario legislature at its recent session, provision was made for the province to meet half the costs of the municipalities' participation in the 1948 rental program. This legislation is very helpful, and should assist in arranging a larger number of units in the province of Ontario than otherwise would have been the case.
In 1947 it became evident that Housing Enterprises could not produce housing at satisfactory cost levels. Housing Enterprises decided to abandon new projects in 1947 and limit their activities to the completion of the 3,313 units under construction. In August, 1947, the life insurance companies which owned Housing Enterprises, approached us to request that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation take over their operations. In light of all circumstances the government accepted this proposal. The corporation has taken over Housing Enterprises Limited and has completed and rented the 3,313 units in the 32 projects.

speechtext:
I could not do that at the moment. I will be glad to do it when we are in committee.
Tba other major form of assistance by the government towards housing construction has been loans under the National Housing Act. It was the largest year in the history of the

act, with 10,933 units being approved. The total figures for the year 1946 appear somewhat larger, but they included the loans made to Housing Enterprises Limited. During the first three months of 1948 activities under the National Housing Act are at new high levels. Loans involving 2,371 units have been approved as compared with 888 units for the first three months of 1947. Although the weather is much further advanced than it was last year, these figures show a great use of the facilities of the act..
Because they do not fall within my department, I will not deal with the other governmental activities in the housing field which include a program of housing for married personnel by the Department of National Defence, small holdings under the Veterans Land Act, and loans for housing purposes under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Canadian Farm Loan Act.
The government is taking vigorous steps in the housing field. I think it should be emphasized that the limitations are physical rather than financial. Effective demand remains very high for home ownership even at present prices. In view of the high rate of family formation, there is an effective demand for rental housing at almost any rental levels. It is difficult to make an estimate of likely accomplishment in 1948. With the large carryover from 1947, I think it is likely that we will equal 1947 completions. Just how far we can exceed this figure is uncertain. On the favourable side there is a better supply of materials, some improvement in the supply of labour, and an undiminished demand for housing. On the unfavourable side there is the increasing lack of serviced land, and a short supply situation in some items such as steel of all kinds. But in my opinion the most unfavourable factor is the continued buoyancy in the cost of construction.
From time to time we receive requests that the corporation increase its level of lending values. We agree that the lending values upon which National Housing Act loans are based are somewhat less than the present average cost of construction. Nevertheless, we do not feel that we would be justified in capitalizing into long term mortgage debt many of the elements of cost which now exist. A further increase in National Housing Act loans would be an inflationary step and would in itself contribute to higher costs. We realize that with the prices of houses rising and no corresponding increase in National Housing Act loans, equity requirements of the home owner are increasing. Nevertheless, after taking all factors into

National Housing Act
consideration, we have decided it would be unwise to contribute further to the general inflationary tendencies, and it is our intention to maintain during 1948 the present level of lending values.
The same problem of high and increasing costs may limit our rental program. Our present policy is that we will not enter into construction of rental units if total costs of all kinds are estimated to exceed $6,800 per unit, which under the rental formula, involves a rental of $37.50 for a five room house. Acceptance of these high costs by us has the effect of confirming the upward trend of prices. We realize that rental housing is needed, but the point has been reached where we must weigh the need for rental housing not only against the very high cost, but also against its contribution to the inflationary trend. Already this difficulty has occurred in municipalities where agreements have already been signed. Our present attitude is that unless arrangements can be made so that a maximum rental level of $37.50 can be maintained, construction will not proceeds
I turn now to the resolution. The proposed amendments to the National Housing Act follow our previous practice of making changes to meet changing situations. The most important of the amendments is the introduction of rental insurance. I have already mentioned that the greatest need in the housing field is for rental housing. The majority of 1947 rental unit completions were by the dominion government. I think that all hon. members will agree that it would be very desirable that there be an increasing supply of rental housing by private enterprise.
The dominion government is in the direct rental housing field because neither private enterprise nor other levels of government is providing greatly needed rental housing accommodation. I look forward to the day when the dominion may withdraw from the field of direct house building. Therefore we are anxious to do everything we can to encourage more private house building. The proposal before the house is designed to make rental housing more attractive to professional landlords and investors.
We have made a careful examination to ascertain the main reason for lack of rental housing by the entrepreneur. A number of builders engaged in the rental field have been interviewed and the whole situation has been thoroughly canvassed. It will be remembered that rentals upon new units are no longer under rental control. Economic rentals in relation to today's costs are readily available. It is our belief that the main deterrent to new 5849-231i
rental construction is the fear that although economic rentals will support present capital costs, the day will come when comparable rental units can be built at a lesser figure, with correspondingly lesser rentals. The builder and the landlord know that economic rentals at today's level will see them through. However, they doubt whether present rentals will be maintained.
We believe that the steps to be taken should have the following characteristics:
1.	Protection to the builder and subsequent owner against an anticipated decline from the economic rentals determined on the basis of present construction -costs.
2.	Provide the builder or owner with some incentive for equity investment.
3.	The arrangement should retain all the traditional debtor-creditor relationship.
4.	The plan should avoid the payment of a subsidy or insurance payments before assistance is needed to protect the position of the owner.
5.	It should be a plan which does not interfere with other forms of credit, particularly in the real estate field.
We therefore intend to introduce a plan of rental insurance. Generally it will guarantee that the owner, whether the builder or a subsequent purchaser, shall be assured of sufficient rental income to look after:
(a)	Taxes.
(b)	Debt service.
(c)	Operating expenses.
(d)	Repairs, renewals and replacements.
(e)	A reasonable return on his equity investment.
Rental insurance will be limited to the class of housing in which we are most interested, family units, renting at not more than $80 per month on a fully serviced basis. Unserviced units would carry lower rental maxi-mums. We will not offer rental insurance in projects which average less than one and a half bedrooms per unit. There will be a requirement that the project consist of eight or more family housing units.
The terms of the contract with the builder will provide that the rents which he' may charge for the first three years shall not exceed the limits which I have already indicated. The contract with the builder will guarantee him annual rentals sufficient to meet charges and to provide a 2 per cent return on the equity investment. I would point out that this is a minimum return to the owner when claims are being made under rental insurance. If the rentals received are above the guaranteed
National Housing Act

rental level, then the owner's return is considerably in excess of 2 per cent. This guaranteed rental will be about 85 per cent of the economic rental which the owner may charge his tenants during the first three years. The owner will pay a premium for his rental insurance at a rate to be set by the governor in council. Provision is made for a lending institution to make loans up to 85 per cent of the estimated cost of the rental housing project. These are to be direct loans with all the funds to be advanced by the lending institution, rather than the usual joint loans under the National Housing Act. It is felt that these high ratio loans are appropriate as investment by lending institutions because, by virtue of the guaranteed rentals, little risk is involved. There should always be sufficient moneys available to service the mortgage debt and pay taxes. Provision is also made that in the event of a loan not being available, then the corporation may make this type of loan. The maximum rate of interest which may be charged on mortgage loans secured by rental insurance will be set by the governor in council. Provision is made for principal repayments of 2i per cent per annum. The loan will be for a period of twenty years.
If the resolution is adopted, more detailed examination of the proposal can be made at the time we are in committee of the whole.
Rental insurance is to meet the fundamental deterrent to a satisfactory volume of new rental housing by private enterprise. It will be recalled that under present National Housing Act loans, guarantees by the government are afforded to the lending institution. This new proposal gives the benefit of such guarantees to the builder or the owner so that he will be willing to enter into rental housing which to his mind is hazardous at this time. On the other hand, the lending institutions will be benefited by the government guarantee because they will be assured that the rental incomes will always be sufficient to meet mortgage payments and taxes.
We are not sure of the amount of new rental housing which will result from this proposal. We hope it will be substantial, and every effort will be made to encourage builders to operate under its provisions. It is likely, however, that most of the new housing will be in the moderate rental field because that is the type of housing in which landlords and builders are interested.
Although the rental insurance provisions will be applicable to rental housing of all types, I do not believe that low rental housing-that is beyond rentals of less than $35 a month- can, be built at this time without substantial capital subsidies or contributions to rent

reduction funds. Because of very high construction costs and because the building industry is now working at capacity, I do not think that the present is an opportune time to attempt initial steps into the low rental housing field. Certainly at this time I am not prepared to recommend capital subsidies or contributions to a rent reduction fund by the dominion.
However, the dominion does not take a dogmatic stand in this matter, and we are willing to discuss with the provinces and municipalities a course of action which would lay a sound foundation for a long term national housing program. The Canadian federation of mayors has already sent us a brief concerning low-rental housing. Their proposals have merit but are not acceptable in their present form chiefly because they contemplate full financing by the dominion government both in respect to capital costs and operating deficits. Whether suitable arrangements for adoption at a more opportune time can be found, I do not know. However, I am quite certain that no suitable arrangements can be found without participation by all three levels of government.
The other main provision in the bill is the winding up of Wartime Housing Limited and the transfer of its assets and liabilities to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The proposal gives the corporation the power to carry out the functions previously performed by Wartime, Housing Limited. It also authorizes the transfer to the corporation of His Majesty's leasehold interest in houses converted under the home conversion plan.
As from January 1, 1947, the corporation has been supplying the management, both for the operation of existing wartime housing units, and the construction of new units. The construction function has been carried on in the name of Wartime Housing Limited. The corporation has been paid a fee for the management of the .wartime housing units. Under the new arrangement, the net revenues from the properties would be payable to the corporation, and would be accounted for pursuant to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act. Hon. members will recall that pursuant to the corporation act, when its reserve fund reaches $5,000,000, all net revenues of the corporation, are payable to the receiver general. We believe that it is desirable to have this new function of the corporation conform to its financial pattern set up by statute. Thus, in place of acting as an agent, it will in the future act as a principal with reference to wartime housing operations, and be subject to account for such

National Housing Act
operations in the same manner as it must account for its lending operations under the other portions of the National Housing Act.
Other powers given to the corporation under this amendment include authority to make title to crown lands. The corporation is at present engaged upon a sale program of certain wartime housing units and it is desirable that they be in a position to convey title rather than relying upon letters patent. Authority is given to the corporation to make payments to municipalities in lieu of taxes.
The other provision is that moneys appropriated by parliament for new construction shall be a liability of the corporation on such terms and conditions as are approved by the Minister of Finance.
The resolution proposes two other measures of somewhat lesser importance. It authorizes lending companies to purchase mortgages or an interest therein from the corporation. These mortgages may result from sale of wartime housing units or from direct loans under section 31A made by the corporation. The purpose of this amendment is to ensure that lending institutions may acquire mortgages from the corporation.
The other change concerns the limited dividend section of the act. Hon. members will recall that little success has attended our efforts in the formation of limited dividend companies to erect rental housing. It has been suggested that if at the end of the amortization period, say forty or fifty years, the owners might have title to the residual value of the property, then this type of limited dividend company might be more attractive to investors. The important feature of the limited dividend section is to provide low rentals for forty or fifty years with a nominal return to owners. If indeed the reversion of the residual value to the shareholders of the limited dividend company will lend encouragement to the development of such companies, I am sure that there will be general agreement that such a change should be made.
We are ' continuing to encourage and assist a large volume of residential construction. It is desirable that private enterprise look after as much of our housing needs as possible. However, to the extent that the housing need is not being met in this way, we are continuing to supplement the over-all program with direct construction. Every effort is being made to see that the improvement in the supply of building materials and building labour is maintained. The provisions of the National Housing Act, including the amendments which are proposed in this resolution, will be vigorously promoted. Our attention is directed particularly to ways and means of increasing the supply of new rental housing units.
Our primary concern is to deal with immediate needs. The long term housing problem, including slum clearance, is one which will require working arrangements with the provinces and the municipalities. It is the earnest desire of the dominion government to do all it can within its constitutional limitations to improve housing conditions. Until some longterm basis can be established with the provinces and municipalities, the dominion is doing what it can within these limitations to alleviate the immediate problem and in particular to discharge its responsibilities for that part of the program that is the direct result of war.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OP APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity we have had this year to debate a problem which is still one of grave concern to the Canadian people, no matter what may be going on throughout the world. The minister has given us an interesting resume of housing activities in Canada. Quite apart, however, from what happened last year, I wish to take this opportunity to indicate a concern which has been in my mind ever since the minister made a speech in Vancouver on October 10,
1947.
I am concerned, and nothing the minister has said today leads me to change my mind, that the minister and the government are quitting their leadership in the housing field. I should like to refer to what the minister said two years ago shortly after he was appointed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as the housing expediter for Canada. I well remember the comprehensive and vigorous speech he made on that occasion, and I remember my own feeling which I expressed at the time that he was really going to go after this problem and solve it. I think he thought that himself. He threw himself into the task, if one can judge from his speeches, with a great deal of energy. I should like to read from page 3690 of Hansard of July 22, 1946, where the minister is reported as follows:
The legislative and administrative steps which I have outlined today give clear indication of a positive and integrated housing policy. This policy is designed primarily to see to the immediate shelter problem, but it does not neglect the long-term implications of the need of raising the standard of housing for people in this country. In conclusion, I would like to sum up the main principles underlying our aims and objects.
(1) High priority. Adequate housing for the Canadian people is one of the major tasks before us. The utmost effort will be directed towards meeting this need, and the resources of the country will be used to this end.
Later on that summer, in a press release in August, the minister talked about the need for
National Homing Act

a definite plan, an organization to implement it and constructive help of all interested in housing needs as the way to meet his objectives. We went on in 1946 and 1947, and the minister set targets of 60,000 and then 80,000, which were met if you take the over-plus from 1946 to make up the deficit in meeting last year's target.
In the meantime a new difficulty added itself to the original problem, which was a shortage of houses and of building materials. The new problem was one of high construction costs and, therefore, one of high rents. A year ago, in February, the minister warned us that the need for rental housing was our chief problem and he put into effect a double depreciation scheme and offered priorities for the building of rental housing. That appears to have failed because, from the minister's own figures, there were only 370 units in respect of which application was made for double depreciation; that is 370 units out of a target of 80,000 and more. It appears, too, from the minister's statement that we have not had much rental housing constructed in the past year. You could see the minister's concern in the speech he made this afternoon that rental housing cannot be provided at rents which the low-income groups most in need of that type of housing can afford to pay. Consequently, when the minister announced in Vancouver his new rental housing policy to take the place of Wartime Housing he rather receded from his enthusiasm of 1946, when he was going to put the whole resources of the country behind a housing drive. He had this to say:
As far as long-term housing program for Canada is concerned, dominion participation must necessarily be indirect, because of the limitations that I have mentioned. The authority lies with the provinces and the dominion can participate directly only when it is invited so to do.
Then he goes on to say:
The principal shortcoming of Canada's housing program to date has been the failure to provide sufficient low-rental housing. To meet this shortage, the active co-operation of dominion, provincial and municipal governments is necessary, since the problem is of such magnitude that no one level of government can see it through alone.
We will all agree with that statement, but not. with this next one:
The responsibility for initiating such a program lies with the provinces.
So we find that in the short space of two years his enthusiastic approach to have this housing problem solved has vanished, and the minister and the government are now crawling under the constitution to get out from the responsibility which the minister assumed

pretty wholeheartedly in 1946. In my view the government is no longer heading the drive for housing but has abdicated its function and is going to do just as little as it must in this field in the future.
I believe that the basic reason for the change in the government's attitude is that it has refused to enter the field of subsidized low-rent housing for those in the low-income group. The minister knows it is not possible to provide rental housing at rents which those in the low-income group can afford to pay, unless this type of housing is subsidized. This is particularly true of veterans, upon whom the present situation bears most heavily, as some figures I shall cite will show. It is not possible to provide housing, unless it is subsidized, at rents which these veterans can pay.
In the face of the rising costs which the minister has mentioned, a rent reduction scheme and a rent reduction fund to be participated in by the three levels of government constitute, in my opinion at least, the only hope for veterans obtaining housing at reasonable rentals.
It was all very well for the minister to say this afternoon that this is not the time, and that the government is not taking a dogmatic stand on this point. I say to him that this is the time to face up to the problem of subsidized low-rent housing. I say that the attitude taken by the government is very dogmatic indeed. I want to call the attention of the house to a statement made recently by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) in a public speech. He said:
No government of which I form a part will ever pass legislation for subsidized housing.

That was a dogmatic and definite statement, and I think it is the mainspring behind the minister's recession from his enthusiasm in approaching this problem two years ago. That statement indicates a fatal refusal to face realities in this field.
There is nothing necessarily socialistic about subsidizing housing for the low-income groups. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and no other minister need ever worry about that. Subsidized housing for those with low incomes was introduced in Great Britain in 1920 by a Conservative government, and it has been in operation, and in useful operation, in the United States of America since 1938 or thereabouts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OP APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister says, "Whenever the costs come down so that it can be made operative." I remember making a speech in this house on housing within the last two years in which I complimented the minister on the provisions he had brought in. I made the criticism that they were all good provisions but were one year late. That has been the record of this government on housing since 1945. In the fall of 1945 we on this side of the house, not only in this party but my hon. friends to my left, all urged the government- the minister was not responsible for housing then-to appoint a housing expediter, to put the whole problem in his hands and to get after it. That was done months after it had been urged from this side of the house. We also urged that special steps be taken to expedite the production of building materials. The minister took those steps one year afterwards.
It is not good enough for the minister to say that this is the wrong time to start building this type of housing. This is the time to concert a plan between the three levels of government concerned and to put it on the statute book and to set up your local building and administration organizations. In my view this is the time to put it into effect as well. Even if the minister is correct today that it would not be the proper time to put the scheme into effect, if we wait until it is right to build before we start negotiations, it will take a whole year even to scratch the surface of all the work that must be done before agreement is reached and houses are actually built.
I want to say a word about the specific measures referred to in the resolution. I say that when the minister has recognized that rental housing is the need, when he recognized it a year ago, and when he recognizes it today, the measures he has brought in now are just puny and entirely inadequate to meet the problem that faces so many people across Canada. I was going to refer to these figures
later, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to draw your attention to the fact that in Vancouver today there are about 4,500 veterans who have active applications for wartime housing on the list. Of these 4,500, 2,000 are married, have families and served overseas. They want wartime housing only because they are not financially able to buy houses, and they cannot rent at S80 a month or something of that kind. Their only hope is through the wartime housing scheme or the minister's new scheme, which, incidentally carries a concealed subsidy in itself, and forces the municipality taking on the scheme to put up some money as well.
The suggestion of the minister that you can solve the rental housing problem for those veterans in particular, who are most in need, by guaranteeing rents and getting rental units built at rents of S80 a month is quite ridiculous. What is needed is an expansion of the scheme that he undertook in Vancouver in October, by which rents up to $37 a month would be charged. Even that amount is high enough for the income group in most difficulty because of the housing shortage. It will not do any good to produce a house at a rental of $80 a month or something like that. There is a sufficient demand for housing by people in that group to take up the lot of it without any filtering down and making houses available to those in lower income groups. I do not believe that in the scheme the minister is proposing today he has added one unit of rental housing for the low-income group person who wants to rent a house.
In his speech the minister said that the limitation on housing is a physical and not a financial one. ll do not think that is true at all. I think there is a definite financial limitation on home ownership today as well as on rental housing, as I have already indicated. The province of Ontario has recognized that fact-the minister commended it a moment ago-and has provided guarantees to lending institutions of part of the prospective home owner's down payment. I believe the guarantee is up to $1,250 a unit. At the same time, in the Ontario Act provision is being made for grants in aid to low-rent housing as well. It may be that all sorts of mortgage money is available in lending institutions, but there certainly is a financial limit on what those seeking new housing can put down as a down payment.
The minister mentioned that the cost of housing had risen; I think he said 15 per cent. The figure I obtained from the report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was 18 per cent over 1946.

Very well. My figures refer to materials and labour, and they have gone up since 1939 a total of 84 per cent to 94 per cent. The minister talks of the average time for completion having been reduced from eleven months to eight months. That is very good indeed; but we must not forget that in 1939 it took only five months to complete a house of a size comparable with the figures given by the minister.
The only new suggestion coming forward from the minister is the idea of stimulating private building of rental housing by means of a guarantee of income. With that in mind, I want to refer for a moment to the situation in my particular city, which I imagine is pretty well typical of any big city in Canada. Earlier I gave the figure of the number of veterans who want wartime housing. I may say that they want wartime housing because they believe it is the only way to get rental housing at a rate that they can afford to pay. That figure is 4,952. At the same time there are 1,500 applications for home conversion units or for emergency shelter units. Therefore, in the city of Vancouver today there are more than 6,000 veterans in the lower income groups who are looking for housing accommodation. When you contrast that with the all-Canada total of 12,000 units, as I understand it, which are contemplated by the minister's new scheme to take the place of wartime housing, you will see that the new plan is just as inadequate as the plan which has been going on for the past two or three years.
I may say that I was quite horrified this afternoon to hear the minister suggest that some of the houses which are proposed to be built under the scheme he announced in Vancouver in October might not be started if building costs continue to rise. We can handle half of them in the city of Vancouver alone. From his figures there are only 1,115 under negotiation in Vancouver, and I should hope that the minister was not talking seriously when he said there was a possibility of a reduction in that number. I should hope the number would be sharply increased if it is possible to get the materials to do so.
The situation in Vancouver with regard to housing is well summed up in a publication of the Vancouver Housing Association entitled "The Housing Situation in Vancouver, Janu-

ary 1948". Under the heading "Over-all Picture", that association says:
Regarded as a whole, the housing situation, in spite of the apparent building activity, has steadily deteriorated during the past year.
It goes on to say:
The city's social service administrator, in his annual report for 1947, states:	"The situation
has greatly deteriorated during the past year. Low-rental housing is not available and social allowances and pensions are so far below the level of economic rentals that it is useless to hope that private landlords will rent quarters at the rates our clients are able to pay."
Later on it points out that, although some 14,800 persons came into the city during the year, the new dwellings completed total only 2,669, and it would take 4,600 houses to handle the newcomers alone.
